# Create reports

URL: https://alexkads.github.io/RavenRS/docs/reporting/
Source: https://github.com/alexkads/RavenRS/blob/master/docs/REPORTING.md

# RavenRS Reporting — design and roadmap

> Status: phase R1 done, 2026-11-01.

RavenRS Reporting turns data into paginated documents. It covers what a complete commercial reporting suite covers: a report engine, a document viewer, exports, an end-user report designer and a report server. Everything is in Rust and runs on desktop, in the browser (WebAssembly) and on servers.

## Goals

* **One engine everywhere.** The same report definition renders identically in the desktop viewer, the browser viewer, a PDF on a server and a test.
* **Reports are data.** A report is a JSON document (`*.rvreport.json`) that can be designed visually, stored in a database, versioned in git and generated by code or AI.
* **Pixel-exact output.** Layout is computed once into a `Document` of positioned primitives in points. Every exporter and the viewer draw that same document.
* **Commercial depth.** The bands, expressions, summaries, master-detail and controls a business report needs (invoices, statements, labels, ledgers, dashboards), with tests and performance budgets like the rest of RavenRS.

## Architecture

```
            report definition (JSON or Rust builder)      data (JSON, Rust structs, SQL, CSV/XLSX)
                              │                                   │
                              ▼                                   ▼
  ravenrs-report ──┬─ ravenrs-criteria ── data binding ── grouping/sorting/summaries
                   └─ ravenrs-graphics ── vector shapes, chart layout, barcodes
        │
        ▼  pagination (Parley text measurement, keep-together, page breaks, can-grow/shrink)
   Document (pages of positioned text, rects, lines, paths, images, links; in points)
        │
        ├── ravenrs-report-export  One entry point for all of these: format, file name, media type
        ├── ravenrs-report-pdf     PDF 1.7 / PDF/A-2b, embedded font subsets, links, outline (pdf-writer + subsetter)
        ├── ravenrs-report-xlsx    XLSX (rust_xlsxwriter), CSV, HTML, SVG/PNG
        ├── ravenrs-report-viewer  DocumentViewer and ParameterPanel: pages, zoom, thumbnails, search
        ├── ReportDesigner         (on the Ribbon): bands, field list, properties, drag and drop, undo/redo
        └── ravenrs-report-server  HTTP: POST a definition + data, get PDF/XLSX back
```

Today `ravenrs-report`, `ravenrs-criteria`, `ravenrs-graphics`, `ravenrs-report-export`, `ravenrs-report-pdf`, `ravenrs-report-xlsx` (XLSX and CSV) and the designer in `examples/report-designer` exist. `ravenrs-report-server` runs them headless ([docs/REPORT-SERVER.md](REPORT-SERVER.md)). `ravenrs-report-viewer` shows documents and asks for parameters. The other exporters arrive in the phases below.

`ravenrs-report` has no GPU or window dependency, so it runs in servers and tests. Text is measured with the same Parley stack as the UI, so the viewer and the PDF agree to the point.

## Report model

* **Page.** Size (A4, Letter, Legal, custom), orientation, margins, watermark (text or image).
* **Bands.**
  * Report: Report Header and Report Footer.
  * Page: Page Header and Page Footer.
  * Groups: Group Header and Group Footer, nested, each with its group field and sort.
  * Detail.
  * Detail Report: master-detail with its own bands, related by key.
  * Band behavior:
    * Keep-together, page break before and after.
    * "Repeat on every page" for headers.
    * Print on first page / last page.
* **Controls.**
  * Text and data:
    * Label, with static text or an expression.
    * Rich Text: simple markup — bold, italic, links, lists.
    * Check Box.
    * Page Info: page `n` of `N`, date, user.
  * Containers:
    * Table, with rows, cells and spans.
    * Panel.
    * Sub-report.
    * Cross-band line and box.
    * Table of contents.
  * Graphics: Picture (PNG, JPEG, SVG), Line, Shape.
  * Barcodes: Code 128, Code 39, EAN-13, EAN-8, UPC-A, ITF, QR, Data Matrix, PDF417.
  * Data visualization:
    * Chart: bar, line, area, pie, doughnut, scatter.
    * Sparkline.
    * Gauge.
    * Cross Tab (pivot).
* **Expressions.** The [`ravenrs-criteria`](../crates/ravenrs-criteria) language, reusable by other modules:
  * Fields and parameters: `[Price] * [Quantity]`, `?Customer`.
  * Conditionals: `Iif([Total] > 1000, 'VIP', 'Regular')`.
  * Aggregates: `Sum([Total])`, `Count()`, `Avg`, `Min`, `Max`, `RunningSum`, scoped to group, page or report.
  * Text and dates: `FormatString('{0:C}', [Total])`, `Today()`, `AddDays`, `Concat`, `Upper` and others.
  * Expressions drive visibility, formatting rules (conditional styles), sorting, filtering and calculated fields.
* **Parameters.**
  * Kinds: typed values (text, number, date, boolean, list).
  * Defaults, required flags and multi-value parameters.
  * The viewer shows a parameter panel.
* **Styles.** Named styles, odd/even rows, conditional formatting. Built-in themes follow the RavenRS tokens and print well.
* **Localization.** Number, date and currency formats per culture (pt-BR first-class); report strings can be translated.

## Data

1. **JSON and Rust structs** (anything `serde::Serialize`), with nested arrays for master-detail.
2. **SQL:** PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server. Each source has queries with parameters, and the report binds to their results. This lives behind a `sql` feature, so the WebAssembly build stays small.
3. **CSV and Excel files.**
4. **Federation:** join several sources and define master-detail relationships between them.

## Delivery phases

Each phase ends with tests, docs, demos and `scripts/check.sh` green, like every RavenRS feature. [REPORTING-PARITY.md](REPORTING-PARITY.md) tracks every feature of a complete reporting suite against these phases.

| Phase | Delivers | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **R1 — Engine and designer preview** | Report model, JSON format with data sources, Rust builder, expressions, parameters, bands, groups, sorting, filtering, summaries, master-detail, pagination, Label/Table/CheckBox/Line/Shape/Panel, styles, pt-BR formats, table wizard, web designer with preview | ✅ 10,000 rows in 80 ms native, about 200 ms in the browser |
| **R2 — PDF and viewer** | PDF export with embedded fonts, links and outline; pictures; viewer with thumbnails and search; full parameter panel (lookups, multi-value); the remaining expression functions | In progress: PDF with embedded fonts, links and outline, and pictures, done (305 pages in about 120 ms, 1 MB); XLSX and CSV moved up from R3 (the same report in about 180 ms). Viewer with thumbnails and search, and a parameter panel, done. Parameter lookups and multi-value wait for the next `YY.1`, since they change a public struct |
| **R3 — Server, scheduling and more output** | `ravenrs-report-server` (see below); XLSX, CSV, HTML, PNG export; barcodes; charts and sparklines; subreports; table of contents; watermarks; multi-column; the remaining band options | In progress: server with storage, render on demand, cron jobs, email and folder delivery, history, retries and retention done; barcodes done, except Data Matrix and PDF417; charts and line sparklines done |
| **R4 — Designer depth** | Expression editor, group and sort panel, snap lines, align and size tools, multi-select, labels wizard, style gallery, drill-down and interactive sorting in preview | Planned |
| **R5 — Enterprise data and documents** | SQL, CSV/XLSX and federated sources; Cross Tab; DOCX; PDF/A, PDF/UA, signatures; vertical bands; right-to-left; AI prompt-to-report | Planned |

## Server and scheduled delivery

`ravenrs-report-server` runs reports headless with the same engine and layouts:

* **Storage.** Layouts (`*.rvreport.json`, data sources included) are stored by the server and versioned; opening and saving them from the designer is planned.
* **Data at run time.**
  * The server resolves `url` data sources when a report runs, only from hosts in its configuration; `sql` sources are planned.
  * Connections and secrets live in the server's configuration, referred to by name, and never in a layout.
* **Render on demand.** An HTTP API: `POST /render` with a layout (or its name), parameters and a format returns PDF or XLSX.
* **Scheduled jobs**, following the job model report servers use:
  * A cron-like schedule.
  * A report and its parameter values, fixed or by expression (for example, last month).
  * Recipients, individually or on one shared email.
  * Delivery as a PDF, XLSX or CSV attachment or a file in a folder; inline HTML and a link are planned.
  * A skip-if-empty option and document retention.
  * A run history of who received what, and retries on failure.

## Decisions

* **Logic that more than one engine can use lives in a shared crate.** `ravenrs-criteria` (expressions), `ravenrs-graphics` (shapes, charts, barcodes) and `ravenrs-report-export` (files) know nothing about who calls them, so reports, the UI and later modules cannot drift apart.
* **Own engine, not a port.** The model uses the concepts report authors already know (bands, criteria-style expressions) so they feel at home, but the format is JSON and the code is ours.
* **`pdf-writer` + `subsetter`** (MIT/Apache, used by Typst) instead of a homemade PDF serializer: proven output, small, no C dependencies.
* **`rust_xlsxwriter`** (MIT/Apache) for XLSX.
* **XLSX cells come from the `Document`, not the data.** A text box keeps the value behind its text, so a spreadsheet gets real numbers and dates on a grid that matches the page. Pages flow into one sheet; the page header prints once and page footers, whose page numbers would mean nothing there, are left out.
* **Points (1/72 in) as the document unit;** the viewer scales to the screen.
* **Layout separate from rendering:** the paginator produces a `Document` once, and the viewer and every exporter consume it, so they cannot drift apart.

## Showing pages elsewhere

`PageFan` (in `ravenrs-report-viewer`) shows real pages of rendered documents spread like a hand of cards, for pages that present reporting: each page is painted once with `paint_page` and reused, opens as the fan scrolls into view, comes forward under the pointer or keyboard focus, and opens its address when clicked.


---

# Report server

URL: https://alexkads.github.io/RavenRS/docs/report-server/
Source: https://github.com/alexkads/RavenRS/blob/master/docs/REPORT-SERVER.md

# Report server

`ravenrs-report-server` runs reports without a UI. It stores layouts with versions, renders them over HTTP, and sends scheduled reports by email or to a folder as PDF, XLSX or CSV. It uses the same engine and exporters as the designer, so a report comes out the same everywhere.

## Run it

Put the configuration in a file:

```json
{
  "listen": "127.0.0.1:8090",
  "dataDir": "/var/lib/ravenrs-reports",
  "outputDir": "/srv/reports",
  "smtp": {
    "host": "smtp.example.com",
    "from": "Reports <reports@example.com>",
    "usernameEnv": "SMTP_USER",
    "passwordEnv": "SMTP_PASSWORD"
  },
  "dataHosts": [
    { "host": "api.example.com", "headersEnv": { "Authorization": "ERP_API_KEY" } }
  ]
}
```

Secrets stay in the environment: the file holds only the names of the variables.

```bash
export RAVENRS_SERVER_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
ravenrs-report-server --config server.json
```

Try it with a sample layout:

```bash
cargo run -p ravenrs-report-server --example sample_layout > invoice.json
```

```bash
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $RAVENRS_SERVER_TOKEN" --data-binary @invoice.json http://127.0.0.1:8090/layouts/invoice
```

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $RAVENRS_SERVER_TOKEN" -d '{"name":"invoice","format":"pdf"}' -o invoice.pdf http://127.0.0.1:8090/render
```

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `listen` | `127.0.0.1:8090` | Address and port |
| `dataDir` | required | Where layouts, jobs, history and kept files live |
| `apiTokenEnv` | `RAVENRS_SERVER_TOKEN` | The variable with the API token, of at least 16 characters; the server does not start without it |
| `outputDir` | none | The folder under which `folder` deliveries write |
| `smtp` | none | The mail server: `host`, `port`, `security` (`starttls`, `tls` or `none`), `from`, `usernameEnv`, `passwordEnv` |
| `dataHosts` | none | The hosts `url` data sources may read, with headers taken from the environment |
| `maxConcurrentRenders` | 4 | Reports rendered at the same time |
| `retryDelaySeconds` | 60 | Wait before the first retry; it doubles on each one |
| `misfireGraceMinutes` | 60 | How late a run may still happen after the server was down |
| `historyLimit` | 1000 | Runs kept per job |
| `maxBodyMegabytes` | 32 | Largest request body |

## Jobs

`PUT /jobs/{id}` with:

```json
{
  "layout": "sales",
  "schedule": "0 8 * * MON",
  "timezone": "America/Recife",
  "parameters": {
    "Region": "Sul",
    "From": { "expression": "AddMonths(Today(), -1)" }
  },
  "formats": ["pdf", "xlsx"],
  "deliveries": [
    {
      "type": "email",
      "to": ["Ana <ana@example.com>", "bruno@example.com"],
      "separately": true,
      "subject": "{report} - {date}",
      "body": "Attached is the report for {date}."
    },
    { "type": "folder", "path": "sales/weekly" }
  ],
  "skipIfEmpty": true,
  "retries": 2,
  "retentionDays": 30,
  "enabled": true
}
```

* **`schedule`** is five cron fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. It takes `*`, lists, ranges, steps and names (`MON`, `JAN`). When both day fields are restricted, a day matches if either does.
* **`timezone`** applies to the schedule and to `Today()`. On a daylight saving change, a local time that clocks skip runs shifted forward, and one that clocks repeat runs once.
* **`parameters`** are fixed values, or expressions in the [criteria language](../crates/ravenrs-criteria) worked out at each run.
* **`separately`** sends one message per recipient, so they do not see each other.
* **`retries`**: a retry renders nothing again and sends only to who did not receive the files.
* **`retentionDays`** keeps each run's files on the server for that long; `0` keeps none. The history stays.

A job always renders the latest version of its layout. The history records which version it was.

| Run status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `success` | Everything was delivered |
| `skippedEmpty` | The report had no rows and `skipIfEmpty` is on |
| `partial` | Some deliveries worked and others did not, after the retries |
| `failed` | Nothing was delivered |
| `missed` | Too late to run after the server was down, or the previous run was still going |

## API

Every route but `/health` needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /health` | Whether the server is up |
| `POST /render` | Renders now. Body: `name` (with an optional `version`) or `layout`; `format`; optional `parameters`, `data`, `timezone`. Answers with the file; `x-report-warnings` counts problems in the report |
| `GET /layouts` | Layout names |
| `PUT /layouts/{name}` | Saves a layout; identical content adds no version. Answers with the version |
| `GET /layouts/{name}` | The latest version, or `?version=n` |
| `GET /layouts/{name}/versions` | Versions and sizes |
| `DELETE /layouts/{name}` | Deletes all versions; refused while a job uses it |
| `GET /jobs`, `GET /jobs/{id}` | Jobs with their next run |
| `PUT /jobs/{id}` | Saves a job after checking it. Answers with its next run |
| `DELETE /jobs/{id}` | Deletes a job with its history and files |
| `POST /jobs/{id}/run` | Runs it now, also when disabled |
| `GET /jobs/{id}/runs` | History, newest first; `?limit=n`, at most 500 |
| `GET /jobs/{id}/runs/{run}` | One run: who received what, errors, report warnings |
| `GET /jobs/{id}/runs/{run}/documents/{file}` | A kept file |

## Data

* **`json`** sources come from the layout, and `POST /render` can send `data` instead.
* **`url`** sources are fetched at each run. `{?Name}` inserts a parameter value, encoded. Only hosts in `dataHosts` can be reached and redirects are not followed, so a layout cannot make the server read its internal network.
* **`sql`** sources are not supported yet, and a run that uses one fails saying so.

## Operating it

* **One identity.** The API token gives full access: there are no users or per-report permissions yet. Anyone with it can read every layout and history, and send email through your server to any address.
* **Keep it private.** It listens on the loopback interface by default and speaks plain HTTP. To reach it from elsewhere, put it behind a proxy with TLS.
* **One instance.** Runs are not coordinated across processes, so two servers on one `dataDir` would send everything twice.
* **At most once.** The next run is saved before a run starts, so a crash cannot repeat a delivery. The run under way when the server stops is not resumed and leaves no history entry.
* **Back up `dataDir`.** It holds everything, as plain files.

## Not built yet

SQL data sources, email with the report inline as HTML, delivery of a link instead of the file, opening and saving layouts on the server from the designer, and users with permissions.


---

# Quality & accessibility

URL: https://alexkads.github.io/RavenRS/docs/quality/
Source: https://github.com/alexkads/RavenRS/blob/master/docs/QUALITY.md

# Quality bar

RavenRS components are meant to be used in production applications, at the level users expect from commercial component vendors. This page defines what "done" means for a component, which checks enforce it, the performance budgets, and where each component stands today.

## Definition of done for a component

A component is ✅ in [PARITY.md](PARITY.md) only when all of these hold:

1. **API.** Typed builder methods with defaults that look right without configuration. Values come in through `Binding<T>`, events go out through closures. Every public item has rustdoc, and the type has a runnable example. Growable enums are `#[non_exhaustive]`.
2. **States.** Rest, hover, pressed, focused (keyboard ring), disabled, selected or checked where it applies, empty, loading and error where it applies, and overflow (long text, many items, a tiny viewport).
3. **Screen readers.** It sets a role and state with `Semantics`, and every control has a name: from its text, a `label`, a `FormField` or a `Tooltip`. The gallery audit (`examples/component-gallery/tests/accessibility.rs`) fails on any unnamed control.
4. **Keyboard.** Reachable with Tab. Enter and Space activate. Arrow keys, Home and End follow the [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/) pattern for that widget. Escape closes overlays.
5. **Themes.** Built only from semantic tokens, so it is correct in Raven Dark, Light and Glass. Text meets WCAG AA contrast, which `ravenrs-style` tests for every theme.
6. **Edge cases.** Empty data, a single item, huge counts, non-ASCII text, out-of-range values (clamped, never panicking) and a zero-size viewport.
7. **Performance.** Meets the [performance contract](#performance-contract) and stays inside the budgets below. Large collections are virtualized.
8. **Tests.** At least one behavior test that drives it through `Ui` (pointer and keyboard). Property tests for any pure logic. A golden image for any component whose drawing is non-trivial.
9. **Docs and demo.** A section in the [component gallery](../examples/component-gallery) that shows its variants and states.

## Enforced checks

`scripts/check.sh --full` runs every check below, and nothing ships unless it passes. The project uses no hosted CI, so this script is the gate. Without `--full` it is the quick check for each pull request: rustfmt, and clippy and the tests of the packages the change reaches (`scripts/changed-packages.py`).

| Check | What it catches |
|---|---|
| `cargo fmt --check` | Formatting drift |
| `cargo clippy -D warnings` on native and `wasm32` | Lints, including `missing_docs` on every public item |
| `cargo test --workspace` | Unit, behavior, accessibility, property ([proptest](https://docs.rs/proptest)) and doc tests |
| GPU golden-image tests (`crates/ravenrs/tests/visual.rs`) | Visual regressions in 6 scenes × dark and light; tolerance 24/255 per channel on at most 0.4% of pixels |
| GPU pixel tests (`crates/ravenrs-render/tests/offscreen.rs`) | Renderer correctness: shapes, clipping, images |
| `cargo doc -D warnings` | Broken intra-doc links |
| `cargo deny check` | Vulnerable, yanked or unlicensed dependencies, and unknown sources |
| `cargo +1.88 check` | The declared minimum Rust version (MSRV) still builds |
| `--no-default-features` | Optional features really are optional |
| `cargo bench --no-run`, only with `RAVENRS_GATE=1` | Benchmarks keep compiling. It runs when asked for, with the performance gate |
| `cargo run --release -p ravenrs-perf -- gate`, only with `RAVENRS_GATE=1` | Performance regressions: the exact work of every scene against `perf/baseline.json`. It runs when asked for, not on every check |
| Web builds | The examples build and bind for WebAssembly |

GPU tests skip themselves, with a message, on machines without a GPU adapter. To accept an intended visual change, regenerate the golden images with `RAVENRS_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test -p ravenrs --test visual`, then review the PNG diff in the commit. A failing run writes `*.actual.png` next to the golden image.

Release checks, run by hand before each publish:
- `cargo semver-checks` against the previous release.
- `cargo llvm-cov` for coverage, at 75% line coverage as of 0.1. Coverage is a signal, not a target.

## Applications built with RavenRS

The rules above that a machine can check also bind applications, through [`ravenrs-lint`](../crates/ravenrs-lint/README.md). It reads an application's syntax tree and denies, like the compiler: literal colors and font sizes, spacing off the 4px grid, button captions without a verb, icon buttons without a name, more than one primary button in a view, `State::new` and blocking work in `body` or `build`, and files over 600 lines. Every rule is an error, and every exception needs a written reason. `cargo ravenrs-lint --init` adds the strictest rustc and Clippy levels, the test that runs the rules on `cargo test`, and the instructions coding agents read; `cargo ravenrs-lint --gate` is the one command that says the work is done.

A rule a machine can check goes into `ravenrs-lint`, not only into this page or the skill.

## Performance method

Optimizing guarantees nothing; a gate that fails on regressions does. There are two instruments, and [the skill](../.claude/skills/ravenrs-desempenho/SKILL.md) is the runbook for both.

**The gate** counts the work of each scene with a real runtime and a real renderer, offscreen: builds, layouts, placements, paints, shaping, allocations in the UI, draw calls and why they split, instances, bytes uploaded, glyphs rasterized, atlas resets. These numbers are exact, so any difference from `perf/baseline.json` fails, improvements included: they have to be accepted with `gate --bless`, which shows up in the diff. Each run repeats itself and fails if the two passes disagree, and it fails without a GPU. On the screens of real applications (`app-*`), allocations are only reported, since they depend on the app's data and the clock. Ceilings in the scene registration keep repeated blessing from eroding the budget. Outside macOS, only ceilings bind. `scripts/perf-plant.py` proves it works by planting regressions.

**Frame time** is measured apart, before each release, with `scripts/perf-time.sh`: the best p99 of three processes, because noise on a laptop almost only adds time. On battery the result is invalid. `ravenrs-perf cold` measures what warm numbers hide, the first time a screen opens.

Budgets for the reference machine, a 14" MacBook Pro with M2 Pro and a 120 Hz screen, at p99:

| Class | CPU | GPU |
|---|---|---|
| Interaction: hover, scroll, animation | 4 ms | 3 ms |
| Rebuild: new data, opening a screen, resizing | 16.67 ms | 3 ms |
| Idle | no frames, no wakes | |

Time is guaranteed only for the registered scenes on that machine. Counters reflect the same logic everywhere, but a latency on another machine does not follow from them. The system compositor is outside the measurement, and Metal's clock is coarse: short passes often read as zero.

### What was measured

On the reference machine at 1280x800 at 2x, with nothing else running. CPU time in milliseconds at p99, per frame:

| Scene | Elements | Hover before | Hover now | Scroll before | Scroll now | Instances before | Instances now | Draw calls before | Draw calls now |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `curve-small` | 105 | 0.90 | 0.36 | 0.05 | 0.05 | 684 | 485 | 61 | 44 |
| `curve-medium` | 1,005 | 5.48 | 2.71 | 0.44 | 0.08 | 6,804 | 482 | 601 | 43 |
| `curve-large` | 10,005 | 59.81 | 30.72 | 5.70 | 0.66 | 68,904 | 482 | 6,001 | 43 |
| `data-grid` | 210 | 1.18 | 0.85 | 1.25 | 0.85 | 644 | 526 | 71 | 62 |
| `scheduler` scroll | 711 | | | 4.56 | 1.41 | 808 | 696 | 452 | 389 |
| `app-finance-dashboard` | 320 | 1.91 | 1.24 | 0.34 | 0.19 | 1,041 | 802 | 116 | 101 |
| `app-finance-entries` | 423 | 1.82 | 1.11 | 1.82 | 1.13 | 1,293 | 1,237 | 118 | 116 |

The "before" column was measured with the same scenes before the work on the core. A Lottie playing went from a rebuild of the whole screen per frame to none. The finance dashboard opening for the second time went from 25.4 ms to 1.1 ms in its worst frame.

The `calculator` scene measures `examples/calculator` as it is, a small screen that stays the same between versions. A click on it, on the same machine: 0.16 ms on the CPU, 0.13 ms recording the GPU's work, 41 instances in 41 draw calls.

Where things stand:

- **Scrolling and animating no longer depend on the size of the screen.** Only what can be seen is painted and sent to the GPU.
- **A rebuild still follows the size of the screen.** About 2.7 µs per element, and layout is now 75% of that. The 4 ms budget holds up to about 1,500 elements. The real screens measured have 200 to 420. Beyond that, the next step would be invalidation by subtree, which changes the API of `View` and `BuildCx`.
- **The GPU is not the bottleneck.** Under 2 ms in every scene.
- **Batching does little on small screens.** Text and shapes alternate, so the calculator needs one draw call per instance. It costs nothing visible today, and painting order would have to be kept by any fix.
- **Resizing a window with charts.** Bars and gridlines are quads now, with no picture to draw or send; a line with more points than columns draws only what can be told apart; and a picture covers only what it draws. The `chart` scenes, dragging the window to a new width each frame, p99 of CPU and of recording the GPU's work, before and after:

  | Scene | CPU before | CPU now | Recording before | Recording now |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | `chart`, a line of 5,000 points | 26.0 | 13.9 | 7.2 | 5.7 |
  | `chart-bars`, three series of 12 bars | 5.5 | 0.1 | 6.3 | 0.1 |
  | `chart-board`, area, bars, doughnut and line | 7.2 | 5.5 | 4.7 | 3.2 |
  | `chart-sankey`, ten flows between ten nodes, as quads and curves | | 0.04 | | 0.1 |

  The finance dashboard went from 19.7 ms to 7.4 ms on the same measure. Lines, areas and slices stay pictures: each scene fits the 16.67 ms of a rebuild, and curves would be drawn again into the atlas on every frame, hover included, at a cost of about 1/26 of a frame per window-sized shape (see below). This comparison was reasoned from those limits, not measured.
- **Not measured:** the delay from input to the screen in a real window, the system compositor, and other machines.
- **Not done:** the gate does not yet fail a public component missing from every scene's `covers`.

### How much the renderer can draw

`ravenrs-perf capacity` grows each kind of work until a frame stops fitting, counting until the GPU finishes, at 2560x1600. On the reference machine:

| Work | Fits at 120 Hz | Fits at 60 Hz | Limited by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rounded quads | 30,000 | 60,000 | GPU |
| Quads with a soft shadow | 4,600 | 9,300 | GPU, the area of the blur |
| Text | 180,000 glyphs | 370,000 glyphs | CPU |
| A quad and a line of 43 glyphs in turn | 1,700 | 3,600 | Both; draw calls about double the cost |
| Quads each with its own clip | 18,000 | 38,000 | Both |
| Small shapes of curves | 6,700 | 13,400 | Both |
| Window-sized shapes of curves | 26 | 56 | GPU |
| Different images | 13,700 | 27,600 | CPU |
| Translucent layers over the whole window | 39 | 81 | GPU |

The real screens measured use 500 to 1,400 instances, so the renderer has about 20 times the room they need. It is not what limits a screen; a rebuild is.

Shapes of curves share a coverage atlas of at most 8192x8192. Past that, the main pass splits to draw another page, so nothing is left out, at the cost of a pass per page.

### Performance contract

Each component answers for these, through a scene in `crates/ravenrs-perf/src/scenes/` listing it in `covers`:

1. **A scene** at its worst realistic case, using only the public API. Simple components can share one.
2. **A class:** static, virtualized, animated or picture.
3. **Scale:** going from N to 10N items, a virtualized component's counters grow at most 1.2 times.
4. **No useless work:** an interaction that does not change text shapes nothing, and an animation builds nothing.
5. **Idle:** no wakes without an animation running or when paused.
6. **Cold cost declared** for a picture: its cache key and what it does with large data.
7. **Ceilings** on draw calls, batch breaks and allocations per interaction.

## Performance budgets

Measured with `cargo bench` (criterion) on an Apple M-series laptop, release profile. Budgets assume a 60 Hz frame (16.7 ms).

| Benchmark | Budget | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Full frame: form with 40 cards (build + layout + paint) | < 8 ms | 1.6 ms |
| Full frame: DataGrid with 100,000 rows | < 8 ms | 2.0 ms |
| Animation frame: the same form, paint phase only | < 2 ms | 0.11 ms |
| DataGrid query over 100k rows: no sort | < 16 ms | 1.0 ms |
| … sort by a number | < 16 ms | 7.9 ms |
| … sort by text, then number | < 16 ms | 12.3 ms |
| … filter row range `100..200` | < 16 ms | 0.9 ms |
| … filter row expression over three conditions | < 16 ms | 8.6 ms |
| … search across columns | < 16 ms | 3.2 ms |
| … group with summaries | < 16 ms | 11.3 ms |
| Shape a label / shape and wrap a paragraph | < 0.1 ms | 0.003 ms / 0.035 ms |
| Report: grouped sales over 10,000 rows, 305 pages | < 300 ms | 80 ms native, about 200 ms in the browser |
| Report: invoice | < 5 ms | 0.05 ms |

Charts are pictures made on the CPU, so their cost is paid when the data or the size changes, and not on other frames: a rebuild that produces the same shapes keeps the same texture. Measured in WebAssembly on Node 24 with the `-Oz` profile, without SIMD, on the same laptop:

| Chart | Median |
|---|---|
| 12 bars, 760x260 at 2x | 4.3 ms |
| Line with 12 points, 760x260 at 2x | 6.1 ms |
| Pie with 8 slices, 360x260 at 2x | 5.3 ms |
| `AreaChart`, 14 values, 760x200 at 2x | 10.8 ms |
| Line with 12 points, 1600x900 at 2x | 22.2 ms |
| Line with 1000 points, 760x260 at 2x | 55.8 ms |
| QR Code, 160 at 2x | 2.1 ms |

Dragging a window's edge redraws every visible chart on each frame, so more than a few at once, or a long series, go over 16.7 ms while it lasts.

The size of a WebAssembly build, after `wasm-opt -Oz`:

| Build | Bytes | Gzipped |
|---|---|---|
| `hello-world`, `charts` off | 2,805,367 | 1,202,999 |
| `hello-world`, `charts` on, not using it | 2,806,628 | 1,203,232 |
| `component-gallery` before charts used it | 3,301,057 | 1,399,745 |
| `component-gallery` using every chart and code | 3,582,964 | 1,504,909 |

Link-time optimization drops what an app does not call, so the feature costs an app without charts about 0.2 KB gzipped. Turning it off saves compile time, not download size. An app that does use charts pays about 105 KB gzipped, its own demos included.

The DataGrid caches the query result and reruns it only when the data or the query changes, so these costs are paid once per user action, not every frame. Version 0.1 broke the budget in three cases (search at 47 ms, filter at 31 ms, text sort at 23 ms). They were fixed by parsing filters once per query, matching text case-insensitively without allocating, computing sort keys only for matching rows, and replacing text comparisons with precomputed ranks.

## Component audit

Status against the definition of done. **Behavior** names the test suites that drive the component. **Visual** marks golden-image coverage. Every component sets screen reader semantics, covered by `accessibility` (widgets) and the gallery audit. Right-to-left layout is missing for every component and is tracked once, in the gaps below.

| Component | Behavior tests | Visual | Keyboard | Notes |

| Lottie | lottie | ✅ decoration unless given `alt`, then an image with that name | n/a | Takes no input; shows its last frame still where motion is reduced, tested. `crates/ravenrs/tests/lottie_corpus.rs` measures real files against lottie-web |

| Dot, OverlayBadge, Rating, IconTile, EmptyState, HeroBanner, MultiProgress, ShimmerText, DaySeparator, ShortcutSheet, ShortcutHintBar, PropertyRow, PageHeader, ZStack, ButtonGroup, FavoriteToggle, SwatchGrid, NinePointAnchor, ColorPair | simple_pieces | | ✅ Rating, SwatchGrid and NinePointAnchor take arrows, the rest Tab and Enter where they act, tested | |
| Media and feedback: Image, Icon, Carousel, Avatar, Badge, Alert, ProgressBar, Spinner, Skeleton, Kbd, Divider | layout_and_content, components, batch_parity | ✅ partial | 🟡 Carousel arrows, untested | |

✅ means the WAI-ARIA keys for that widget work and a test covers them. 🟡 means it is reachable and activatable but the full pattern is missing or untested.

Defects found and fixed during this audit:
- RadioGroup, SegmentedControl and Stepper had no keyboard support beyond Tab. Tabs, ToggleGroup, every menu, the Select list and the Calendar grid lacked their arrow-key patterns, and Calendar days could not take focus at all.
- Tab could leave an open Dialog or Sheet for the page behind it; focus now stays inside and returns to the opener on close.
- Focus moved by code hid the focus ring even when the user was navigating by keyboard.
- `AspectRatio` content with modifiers (for example `Spacer::new().background(...)`) collapsed to zero height.
- The DataGrid query exceeded the frame budget on 100k rows (see above).

## Known gaps

These block a "commercial-grade" label and are prioritized ahead of new components of the same family:

1. **Right-to-left layout.** Parley shapes bidirectional text, but layouts do not mirror.
2. **Remaining keyboard patterns** in the 🟡 rows above: Ribbon key tips.
3. **Visual coverage.** Golden images exist for 7 scenes. Overlays and navigation have none yet.
4. **Screen reader depth.** Text fields do not expose caret position or selection, and the web mirror is rebuilt whole when the tree changes. Tested with macOS VoiceOver's API (System Events) and the browser's DOM; not yet with NVDA, Narrator or Orca.

# Performance

URL: https://alexkads.github.io/RavenRS/docs/performance/
Source: https://github.com/alexkads/RavenRS/blob/master/docs/PERFORMANCE.md

# Finding out why a screen is slow

This guide is for anyone using RavenRS. Budgets, and how the library keeps to them, are in [QUALITY.md](QUALITY.md).

## Open the panel

Press Ctrl+Shift+D, or Cmd+Shift+D on a Mac, in any app. On the desktop, `RAVENRS_DIAG=1` also opens it at start. While it is closed, none of this costs anything. While it is open, it also measures itself, so expect slightly higher numbers.

## Read it in this order

**1. Latest frames.** Each bar is a frame, split by where its time went: views, layout, paint, GPU work and waiting. The line across is the 120 Hz budget. Bars under the line are fine. If only a few spikes cross it, look at what you were doing at that moment.

**2. Why the screen was rebuilt.** Each rebuild runs every view on the screen, so its cost follows the size of the screen. This list says what caused them:

| Cause | What to check |
|---|---|
| Data changed | A `State` is being set more often than it changes. Use `set_if_changed`. |
| Pointer moved | Normal for views that ask `is_hovered`. Do not ask unless the view looks different. |
| A view's timer | `wake_at` rebuilds everything. For drawing that moves, use `Paint::Live`, which repeats only the painting. |
| Scrolled | Expected for a virtualized list, not for plain content. |

**3. Costliest views.** The types of view that took the longest in the latest build, without counting the views inside them. Your own components appear under their own names. If one is at the top, look for work done in `build` that could happen once.

**4. Draw calls split by.** Text and shapes alternating split them by kind, which is normal. Many splits by image mean many separate images on screen.

**5. GPU resources.** Atlas resets should stop once the screen has been shown. If they keep rising, too many different glyph sizes are in use.

## Take a capture

"Copy capture for Perfetto" copies the latest frames. Save them to a `.json` file and open it at <https://ui.perfetto.dev> to see every phase on a timeline, or attach it to a bug report.

## What makes a screen cheap

- **Rebuilds are the expensive thing.** They cost about 3 µs per element on a recent laptop, most of it in layout. Scrolling and animating do not rebuild, unless a view asks to.
- **What is off screen costs little.** It is built and laid out but not painted, so a long list scrolls smoothly. Beyond about a thousand elements, use a virtualized view such as `DataGrid`, because each rebuild still runs them all.
- **Text is shaped once.** The same text in the same style is reused between rebuilds, so showing a changing number costs little.
- **Charts are pictures.** Their cost comes when their data or size changes. One that returns unchanged is not drawn again.

## Measuring in this repository

See [the runbook](../.claude/skills/ravenrs-desempenho/SKILL.md).

# Versions & upgrades

URL: https://alexkads.github.io/RavenRS/docs/versioning/
Source: https://github.com/alexkads/RavenRS/blob/master/docs/VERSIONING.md

# Versioning and releases

> Adopted on 2026-10-31. The first release under this model is 26.2.0, which follows 0.1.0.

RavenRS follows the release model of commercial component vendors, adapted so that every version is also valid [Cargo SemVer](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html).

## The version number: `YY.R.P`

| Part | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `YY` | Year of the major release. The only place where breaking changes happen. | `27` |
| `R` | Feature release within the year: 1 in the first half, 2 in the second. Additions only. | `27.1` |
| `P` | Maintenance release: fixes, performance and documentation. Monthly, or sooner for serious bugs. | `27.1.3` |

Commercial component vendors name releases the same way, such as `25.1` and `25.2`, or `2025.1`. The difference is that in RavenRS, `27.1 → 27.2` never breaks your build. `ravenrs = "27"` in `Cargo.toml` follows every feature and maintenance release of that year automatically. Breaking changes wait for the next year's `.1` release, from 28.1.0 on: see below for what holds until then.

## Calendar

A breaking change can bring a `YY.1.0` forward rather than slip into a feature release: 27.1.0 shipped in November 2026 for that reason. That was the last time: **`YY` and `R` now follow the calendar only**. Until 27.2.0, in the second half of 2027, every release is the next `27.1.P`.

**Until 28.1.0, any release may hold breaking changes**, listed under *Breaking* in the CHANGELOG. The library is still taking shape, and holding its API still costs more than it saves. So until then `ravenrs = "27"` can break your build on `cargo update`: pin an exact version, `ravenrs = "=27.1.8"`, if that matters to you. The table below is what holds from 28.1.0 on.

| When | Release | What it may contain |
|---|---|---|
| First half of the year | `YY.1.0` | New components and features, **and** the year's breaking changes, each listed in a migration guide |
| Second half of the year | `YY.2.0` | New components and features only |
| Monthly | `YY.R.P` | Fixes only |

Each feature release has a public beta (`YY.R.0-beta.N`) about four weeks before the final release.

## Support

- The current year's line gets fixes. The previous year's line gets security and critical fixes for 12 months after the next major ships.
- **MSRV.** A feature release may raise the minimum Rust version to one at least six months old. A maintenance release never raises it.
- Deprecations are announced in a feature release with `#[deprecated]` and a replacement, and are removed no earlier than the next major.

## What counts as breaking

Breaking changes are the ones that Cargo SemVer and [`cargo semver-checks`](https://github.com/obi1kenobi/cargo-semver-checks) treat as major. Enums that grow are `#[non_exhaustive]`, and builders have defaults, so new variants, fields and options are additions. Visual changes count too: a change that moves pixels in the golden-image tests ships only in a feature or major release, with a CHANGELOG entry.

## Release checklist

1. `scripts/check.sh --full` passes, including the golden-image tests.
2. `cargo semver-checks` runs against the previous release. Until 28.1.0, what it finds goes under *Breaking* in the CHANGELOG; from then on it has to agree with the version bump.
3. Benchmarks are within the budgets in [QUALITY.md](QUALITY.md).
4. CHANGELOG has an entry, plus a migration guide for a major.
5. All crates are published in dependency order, then the tag `vYY.R.P`, the GitHub release, and the site and API docs are updated.
6. Every crate's documentation built on docs.rs (`https://docs.rs/crate/<name>/<version>/status.json`); it uses a recent nightly, so it can fail when stable passes.

## npm preparer patches

`npm/create-ravenrs/release.json` pins the Rust CLI version and Git tag used by the preparer.
An npm-only documentation or installer patch can increment the npm patch version while
keeping that Rust pin. The major and minor versions must match and the npm patch cannot
be below the framework patch. `--version` reports both versions.

For an npm-only release, increment `package.json` and its lockfile, run the Node tests and
`npm run prepack --prefix npm/create-ravenrs`, inspect `npm pack --dry-run`, then publish
from the package directory. Do not create a Rust `vYY.R.P` tag for an npm-only patch.
For a new framework release, run `prepare-release` and ensure the npm version is unpublished
before publishing. The prepack guard checks the pinned workspace release and toolchain;
it does not query the registry for previously published versions.
